title: Asking for Directions in Spanish: Phrases and Answers

body_html:
Asking for directions in Spanish is easy; understanding the answer is the hard part. The question itself takes one polite opening and one phrase: Disculpe, ¿dónde está el metro? The answer, though, often comes quickly, with gestures, landmarks and words like cuadra, esquina and derecho. This guide covers both sides: how to ask, and how to follow what people tell you, with the regional words you will hear in Mexico and Spain.

Quick answer
  • Ask: Disculpe, ¿dónde está…? ¿Cómo llego a…?
  • Distance: ¿Está lejos? ¿Se puede ir caminando?
  • Answers: a la derecha, a la izquierda, todo derecho, a dos cuadras
  • If lost: ¿Me lo puede repetir más despacio?
{{toc}}

Asking for directions in Spanish: the key questions

SpanishEnglish
Disculpe, ¿dónde está la estación?Excuse me, where is the station?
¿Cómo llego al centro?How do I get downtown?
¿Hay una farmacia por aquí?Is there a pharmacy around here?
¿Está lejos?Is it far?
¿Se puede ir caminando?Can you walk there?
¿Cuánto tiempo se hace caminando?How long does it take on foot?
¿Me lo puede enseñar en el mapa?Could you show me on the map?
Estoy perdido.I’m lost. (perdida if you are female)

Start with Disculpe or Perdone to get someone’s attention politely. With young people or in very casual settings, Oye, ¿sabes dónde está…? is fine.

Understanding the answer

SpanishEnglish
Siga todo derecho.Go straight ahead. (Spain: todo recto)
Dé vuelta a la derecha.Turn right. (Spain: gire a la derecha)
Dé vuelta a la izquierda.Turn left.
En la esquina.On the corner.
A dos cuadras.Two blocks away. (Spain: a dos manzanas)
Enfrente de la iglesia.Across from the church.
Al lado del banco.Next to the bank.
Al final de la calle.At the end of the street.
Pasando el semáforo.Past the traffic light.
Está a cinco minutos.It’s five minutes away.

Notice the formal commands: siga, dé vuelta, cruce (cross), tome (take). People giving directions often use usted forms with strangers.

{{image:2}}

Landmarks and places

Directions in Spanish-speaking cities often rely on landmarks rather than street names. Useful words:

  • la plaza the square, el zócalo the main square (Mexico)
  • el semáforo the traffic light, la glorieta the traffic circle (Mexico; Spain: la rotonda)
  • la parada de autobús the bus stop, la estación de metro the subway station
  • el puente the bridge, la avenida the avenue, la calle the street
  • el Oxxo the convenience store (a very common landmark in Mexico)

In Mexico, someone might tell you Está pasando el Oxxo, a mano derecha (It’s past the Oxxo, on the right-hand side).

A sample conversation

Tú: Disculpe, ¿sabe dónde está el Museo Frida Kahlo?
Excuse me, do you know where the Frida Kahlo Museum is?

Señora: Sí, está cerca. Siga derecho por esta calle tres cuadras.
Yes, it’s close. Go straight along this street for three blocks.

Tú: ¿Tres cuadras?
Three blocks?

Señora: Sí. Luego da vuelta a la izquierda en la esquina de la farmacia. Ahí está, es una casa azul.
Yes. Then turn left at the corner with the pharmacy. It’s right there, a blue house.

Tú: Muchas gracias, muy amable.
Thank you very much, that’s very kind.

Repeating a key detail as a question (¿Tres cuadras?) is a natural way to check you understood, and it gives the other person a chance to slow down.

{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

When you don’t understand

Nobody understands every set of directions the first time, even in their own language. These phrases help:

  • ¿Me lo puede repetir más despacio, por favor? Could you repeat that more slowly, please?
  • Entonces, ¿derecho y luego a la derecha? So, straight and then right?
  • ¿Me lo puede escribir? Could you write it down for me?
  • ¿Hay algún lugar conocido cerca? Is there a well-known place nearby?

It is also wise to ask a second person. People often prefer to give directions rather than admit they don’t know, so a friendly double-check saves time. For more survival phrases, see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

Getting there by transport

  • ¿Qué camión me lleva al centro? Which bus takes me downtown? (In Mexico, a city bus is often a camión.)
  • ¿En qué estación me bajo? Which station do I get off at?
  • ¿Tengo que transbordar? Do I have to transfer?
  • ¿Este metro va a…? Does this train go to…?

For taxis and ride apps, see {{link:taking-a-taxi-in-spanish|taking a taxi in Spanish}}. Mexico City’s official metro site, Metro CDMX, has maps and route planning in Spanish, which is good reading practice before your trip.

{{image:3}}

Common mistakes

  • ¿Dónde es el museo? For location, use estar: ¿Dónde está el museo? (Events use ser: ¿Dónde es la fiesta?) See {{link:ser-vs-estar|ser vs estar}}.
  • Confusing derecho and derecha. Derecho means straight ahead; a la derecha means to the right.
  • ¿Puede decirme el camino a…? Correct, but ¿Cómo llego a…? is what people really say.
  • Forgetting a: ¿Cómo llego el hotel? It is ¿Cómo llego al hotel?
{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Asking for directions in Spanish is a perfect beginner conversation: short, useful and full of words you will hear again. Learn the questions, practice the answer words until you can picture them, and don’t be shy about asking someone to repeat. For more travel and everyday moments, see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

faq.q: How do you ask for directions politely in Spanish?
faq.a: Start with Disculpe and ask ¿dónde está…? or ¿cómo llego a…?

faq.q: What is the difference between derecho and derecha?
faq.a: Derecho means straight ahead; a la derecha means to the right.

faq.q: How do you say “block” in Spanish?
faq.a: Cuadra in Mexico and most of Latin America, manzana in Spain.

faq.q: What if I don’t understand the directions?
faq.a: Ask ¿Me lo puede repetir más despacio?, repeat the key points back, or ask the person to show you on a map.

questions.explain: To the right is a la derecha.

questions.q: “How do I get to the hotel?”
questions.explain: Llegar a, and a + el = al.

questions.q: In Mexico, a city bus is often called…
questions.explain: Guagua is used in the Caribbean and the Canary Islands.
